lessons.title: Installing Claude Code
lessons.bodyMd:
## What you are installing

Claude Code is Anthropic's official coding agent. It runs in your terminal or inside your editor, and unlike a chat window, it can actually read your files, run commands, edit code, and run tests. Think of it as a junior developer who sits inside your machine, has perfect memory of every file, and never gets tired.

There are two ways to get it: the terminal install (fast, powerful, recommended) and the editor extension (visual, friendly). This lesson covers the terminal path. The editor path comes later in this chapter.

## Step 1: Check your requirements

Before installing, make sure you have:

- A Mac, Linux machine, or Windows with WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux)
- Node.js 18 or newer installed (Claude Code runs on Node under the hood)
- An Anthropic account with at least the Pro plan

You can check Node with one command:

```bash
node --version
```

If that prints something like `v20.11.0`, you are good. If you get "command not found", install Node from nodejs.org first, then come back here.

## Step 2: Run the installer

Open your terminal and run the official install script:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://claude.code.com/install | bash
```

This downloads Claude Code, puts it on your system path, and wires it up. The whole thing takes under a minute on a decent connection.

Once it finishes, verify it worked:

```bash
claude --version
```

You should see a version number like `1.0.42`. If your terminal says "command not found", close the terminal, open a fresh one, and try again. New shells pick up path changes that old ones miss.

## Step 3: Update regularly

Claude Code ships updates constantly. New models, new features, and bug fixes land every week. Make it a habit to check for updates:

```bash
claude update
```

A good rhythm is to run this every Monday morning before you start work. Outdated versions occasionally hit API changes that break things in confusing ways, and a fresh update fixes most of those instantly.

## What about Windows without WSL?

Claude Code is designed for Unix-style shells. If you are on Windows, install WSL2 first (Ubuntu is the default and works great), then do everything above inside the WSL terminal. The experience inside WSL is identical to native Linux, and all your files in the WSL filesystem are fair game for the agent.

## Common install hiccups

**"Permission denied" during install.** Try the install again without piping to a privileged location, or check that `~/.local/bin` is writable. Do not reach for `sudo` as a first instinct; user-level installs are safer and easier to update.

**Corporate proxy blocks the download.** If you are behind a work proxy, set the standard proxy environment variables (`HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY`) in your shell before running the installer.

**Version command works but `claude` fails in a project.** That is usually an auth issue, not an install issue. The next lesson walks through authentication.

## Key takeaway

Installation is a two minute job: check Node, run the script, verify the version. Keep it updated weekly. Everything else in this guide assumes this step is done, so get it solid before moving on.

lessons.title: Authentication and Plans
lessons.bodyMd:
## Why auth matters

Claude Code is powered by real Anthropic models running in the cloud. Every prompt you send uses compute on Anthropic's servers, so you need an account and a paid plan before the tool will talk to you. This lesson covers logging in and picking the right plan.

## First-time login

Type `claude` in your terminal to launch the tool. The very first time, it will ask you to authenticate. Run the login command:

```
/login
```

This opens your browser to Anthropic's sign-in page. Log in with your Anthropic account, approve the connection, and come back to the terminal. Claude Code stores a secure token locally so you only do this dance once; future sessions just work.

If the browser does not open automatically, Claude Code prints a URL you can paste into any browser yourself. Handy when you are working over SSH on a remote machine.

## Plan requirements

Claude Code requires a paid Anthropic plan. The Pro plan (around $17 per month at the time of writing) is the entry point. The free tier does not include Claude Code access.

Which plan should you pick? For learning and side projects, Pro is plenty. You get generous usage limits that cover a full day of building for most people. If you find yourself hitting usage caps regularly, the higher tiers raise those caps. Start with Pro and upgrade only when the limits actually slow you down.

## Checking your account

Inside a Claude Code session you can run:

```
/account
```

This shows your current plan, account email, and usage status. When something feels off (rate limits, unexpected errors), this is the first place to look.

## Token storage and security

Your login token lives in your home directory's config folder. Treat it like a password:

- Never paste it into chat, forums, or public repos
- Never commit it to git (it lives outside your project folders by default, which helps)
- If you suspect it leaked, log out and back in to rotate it

You can log out with `/logout` inside Claude Code. Logging out wipes the local token immediately.

## Switching accounts

Some people keep a personal account and a work account. Claude Code supports one active login at a time. To switch, run `/logout`, then `/login` again with the other account. If you constantly switch, consider running separate OS user profiles to keep the tokens isolated.

## What "authenticated" unlocks

Once logged in, a bare `claude` launch drops you into an interactive session in your current folder. From there you can ask questions about the codebase, request edits, run tests, and use every slash command covered later in this guide. Authentication is the gate; everything after it is just workflow.

Claude Code defaults to Sonnet 5, Anthropic's most agentic Sonnet model, so you start on the best-value model out of the box. The Core Workflow chapter has a full lesson on choosing your model for the rare cases when you need something different.

## Troubleshooting login

**Browser opens but terminal hangs.** The auth flow waits for a callback. If your browser and terminal are on different machines (SSH), use the printed URL method instead.

**"Plan not eligible" error.** Double check you are logged into the right Anthropic account and that the subscription is active. Trial or expired subscriptions trigger this.

**Token expired mid-session.** Rare, but it happens after long idle periods. Just run `/login` again.

## Key takeaway

Run `/login` once, confirm you are on at least the Pro plan, and check `/account` when in doubt. Guard your token like a password. Auth is boring on purpose; set it up and forget about it.

lessons.title: Terminal vs VS Code vs Anti-gravity
lessons.bodyMd:
## Three doors into the same engine

Claude Code is one engine with three front doors: the raw terminal, the VS Code extension, and Anti-gravity (Google's AI-first editor, essentially VS Code 2.0). They all talk to the same models. The difference is the experience around them. This lesson helps you pick your starting point and understand what each one is good at.

## The terminal: raw and powerful

Type `claude` in any folder and you get the full agent in your shell. Why do experienced users love it?

- **Fastest refresh times.** No GUI overhead between you and the model.
- **Custom status line.** A live bar showing context usage, current model, and git branch, configured to your taste.
- **Multiple instances side by side.** Open three terminal tabs, run three agents on three tasks.
- **Slash commands and fast mode.** The full command surface is one keystroke away.
- **More hackable.** Pipes, scripts, and shell integration work naturally.

The tradeoff is approachability. You live in text, diffs render in the terminal, and there is no click-to-open file tree. If you are comfortable in a shell, this is home.

## VS Code: the friendly middle ground

Install the official **Claude Code for VS Code** extension published by Anthropic (look for the verified publisher checkmark). Open the command palette, find the Claude panel, or click the Claude icon in the top right.

Why beginners like it:

- **Visual file context.** You see exactly which files the agent is looking at.
- **Built-in thinking tab.** Watch the agent's reasoning unfold in a readable panel.
- **Approachable for simple edits.** Click, review the diff, accept.

Watch out for impostors. There are fake extensions with similar names in the marketplace. Only install the one published by Anthropic with the verification checkmark. A fake extension can steal your auth token.

## Anti-gravity: the AI-first option

Anti-gravity is Google's modern take on the code editor, built AI-first from the ground up. The setup mirrors VS Code: install the Claude Code for VS Code extension inside Anti-gravity, then click the Claude icon to replace the default Gemini agent panel with Claude.

It feels like VS Code with the rough edges sanded off: cleaner agent panels, smoother context handling, and a more modern shell. If you like VS Code's approach but want something fresher, this is worth a try.

## Head to head

| | Terminal | VS Code | Anti-gravity |
|---|---|---|---|
| Speed | Fastest | Medium | Medium |
| Learning curve | Steeper | Gentle | Gentle |
| Multi-instance | Trivial (tabs) | Possible (panels) | Possible (panels) |
| Visual diffs | Text-based | Rich | Rich |
| Customization | Maximum | Good | Good |
| Best for | Power users, scripting | Everyday development | Modern AI-first feel |

## Our recommendation

Learn the terminal first. It unlocks the most functionality: the full slash command set, the status line, headless scripting (covered in Chapter 6), and the fastest iteration loop. Once you are comfortable there, add the VS Code or Anti-gravity extension for visual tasks like UI iteration, where seeing the design matters.

You are not locked in. Many developers use the terminal for backend work and the GUI for frontend polish in the same afternoon. The underlying agent is identical, so skills and habits transfer.

## Setting up the GUI path

1. Install VS Code or Anti-gravity from their official sites.
2. Open the extensions marketplace inside the editor.
3. Search "Claude Code", verify the publisher is Anthropic, install.
4. Open a project folder, click the Claude icon, and run `/login` if prompted.

That is it. The extension reuses your terminal auth token, so you do not log in twice.

## Key takeaway

Same engine, three doors. Start with the terminal to learn the full tool, add a GUI for visual work. Verify the extension publisher to avoid fakes. Mix and match freely once you are comfortable.

lessons.title: Your First Session
lessons.bodyMd:
## Opening the door

Open your terminal, navigate to a project folder (or an empty folder for practice), and type:

```bash
cd ~/projects/my-app
claude
```

Claude Code greets you and waits. You are now in an interactive session. Everything you type goes to the model with full awareness of the folder you launched in. Try your first prompt:

```
What is in this folder? Give me a quick overview of the project structure.
```

Watch what happens. Claude lists files, reads the important ones, and summarizes. Notice it did not ask you to paste anything; it went and looked itself. That is the fundamental shift from chatbots to agents: it has hands, not just words.

## Your first real task

Now give it something slightly bigger. A great first exercise is documentation:

```
Read the main entry files and write a short README.md explaining what this
project does, how to install it, and how to run it. Ask me before writing
any files.
```

Two things to notice. First, you gave it a concrete, bounded task. Second, you set a permission boundary ("ask me before writing any files"). Claude will research, then pause for approval before creating anything. This is how you stay in control while the agent does the legwork.

## How the agent shows its work

During a task, Claude Code narrates: which files it reads, what it is thinking, and what it plans to do. When it wants to change a file, it shows you a diff, the exact lines being added and removed, before applying it (depending on your permission mode, covered in Chapter 2).

Get in the habit of reading these narrations, especially early on. They teach you how the agent thinks, which makes your future prompts sharper. You start to learn what details help it and what details just add noise.

## Ending and resuming

To leave a session, type `exit` or press Ctrl+C twice. Your conversation history for that folder is saved automatically. Launch `claude` in the same folder later and you can pick up where you left off with the `-c` (continue) flag:

```bash
claude -c
```

This resumes your most recent session in that directory. It is perfect for multi-day projects: close the laptop, come back tomorrow, continue the same thread.

## The resume flag family

- `claude` starts a fresh session
- `claude -c` continues the most recent session
- `claude -r` shows a picker of past sessions to resume

Use `-c` liberally during active projects. Starting fresh every time forces the agent to re-learn your codebase from zero, which burns context and time.

## A practice drill

Do this once, in an empty folder, to build muscle memory:

1. `mkdir claude-practice && cd claude-practice`
2. `claude`
3. Ask: "Create a simple Python script that prints the first 10 Fibonacci numbers, then run it to verify the output."
4. Review the diff, approve it, watch it run.
5. Type `exit`, then `claude -c` to resume and ask: "Now add a function that returns the nth Fibonacci number and test it."

That five minute drill teaches you the whole loop: prompt, review, approve, verify, resume. Every advanced technique in this guide is a variation on that loop.

## Key takeaway

Launch with `claude`, start with small bounded tasks, read the agent's narration, and use `claude -c` to resume. Do the practice drill once. You now know enough to be dangerous; the next chapters make you effective.

lessons.title: How a Session Works
lessons.bodyMd:
## The anatomy of a session

A Claude Code session is a loop between you and the agent, and understanding the loop is what separates people who fight the tool from people who fly with it. Here is what actually happens when you send a prompt:

1. **You describe the task.** One message, as specific as you can make it.
2. **Claude explores.** It reads files, searches the codebase, maybe runs commands to understand the current state.
3. **Claude proposes or acts.** Depending on your permission mode, it either shows you a plan or starts making changes.
4. **You review.** Read the diffs, check the reasoning, catch mistakes early.
5. **Claude verifies.** It runs tests, builds, or lints to prove the change works.
6. **Repeat** until the task is done.

Steps 2 through 5 are where beginners go wrong. They skip the review, or they never ask for verification, and then they wonder why the code "mostly works" but breaks in production.

## Prompt like a manager, not a micromanager

The best prompts give the agent a clear goal and the context it needs, then get out of the way. Compare:

Weak:
```
Fix the bug.
```

Strong:
```
The login form on /login returns a 500 when the email field is empty.
The relevant files are probably in src/auth/. Reproduce it first if you
can, fix it, then run the auth test suite to confirm nothing broke.
```

The strong prompt names the symptom, points at the neighborhood, and demands verification. The agent still does the detective work, but it starts in the right zip code.

## One task per message

Resist the urge to stack five requests into one prompt. Long compound prompts dilute focus; the agent does a mediocre job on all five instead of a great job on one. Send one task, let it finish, then send the next. You will actually go faster, because each result is good enough to build on.

When tasks genuinely depend on each other, say so explicitly:

```
First fix the login 500. Once the tests pass, add validation so the
email field shows an inline error instead of submitting empty.
```

## The session has memory, use it

Everything in the current session is shared context. You do not need to re-explain the project in every message. Reference earlier work naturally:

```
The validation approach you used on the login form, apply the same
pattern to the signup form.
```

This is also why `claude -c` (resume) matters from Chapter 1. Continuing a session preserves all that shared understanding. Starting fresh throws it away.

## Watch for the drift

Long sessions drift. After 30 or 40 messages, the agent's early context gets compressed (more on this in Chapter 3), and it may start making choices that contradict decisions from an hour ago. Signs of drift:

- It re-asks questions you already answered
- It suggests approaches you already rejected
- Code style subtly changes mid-session

The fix is simple: start a fresh session for the new task, or run `/compact` to compress the conversation deliberately and restate your key constraints in the next message. A two sentence recap ("We decided to use Zod for validation and Tailwind for styling") re-anchors everything.

## Interrupting is fine

If Claude starts going down the wrong path, you do not have to wait. Press Escape to stop it mid-stream, correct course, and send a new prompt. Interrupting early saves far more time than letting a bad approach run to completion and then undoing it. Think of it like pair programming: you would tap your partner on the shoulder, not watch silently for twenty minutes.

## Key takeaway

A session is a loop: specific prompt, agent explores, you review, agent verifies, repeat. One task per message, leverage session memory, interrupt early when it drifts, and restart or compact when the thread gets long.

lessons.title: Reading, Editing, and Diffs
lessons.bodyMd:
## Files are the interface

Everything Claude Code does flows through files. It reads them to understand, edits them to build, and shows you diffs so you can review. Getting comfortable with this file-centric workflow is the core skill of the whole tool.

## How Claude reads your project

When you ask a question, Claude does not guess from the prompt alone. It uses read and search tools to pull in the actual files. You will see narration like "Reading src/auth/login.ts" as it works. For big questions it may scan dozens of files in seconds, something that would take you half an hour of clicking around.

You can point it at specific files to save time:

```
Explain how authentication works. Start with src/auth/session.ts
and follow the imports from there.
```

Naming the entry point focuses the exploration. Without it, Claude still finds its way, but it burns more context getting oriented.

## Diffs: your review superpower

When Claude edits a file, it shows you a diff before applying the change (in the default permission mode). A diff shows removed lines with a minus sign and added lines with a plus sign:

```diff
 function validateEmail(email) {
-  return email.includes('@');
+  if (!email || typeof email !== 'string') return false;
+  return /^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/.test(email);
 }
```

Reading diffs is a skill worth practicing deliberately. For every change, ask yourself three questions:

1. **Does it do what I asked?** Check the actual logic, not just the narration.
2. **Did it touch anything I did not ask about?** Scope creep in edits is the most common agent mistake.
3. **Would I be embarrassed if this shipped?** Style, naming, comments.

Early on, review every diff carefully. As you build trust with the tool on a given codebase, you can skim the small ones and focus on the risky ones.

## Asking for targeted edits

Vague edit requests produce vague edits. Be surgical:

```
In src/components/Button.tsx, change the primary variant's background
from blue-600 to navy-900. Don't touch anything else in the file.
```

The "don't touch anything else" clause matters. Agents love to "helpfully" reformat neighboring code, fix unrelated typos, or upgrade a dependency while they are in there. Explicit scoping keeps diffs clean and reviewable.

## When edits go wrong

It happens. The agent misreads your intent, edits the wrong file, or introduces a bug. You have options, in order of escalation:

1. **Say what is wrong plainly.** "That broke the mobile layout, the button now overflows on small screens." The agent can usually fix its own mistakes when you describe the symptom.
2. **Ask it to revert.** "Revert your last change to Button.tsx." Claude tracks its edits and can undo them.
3. **Revert with git.** If things are truly tangled, `git checkout -- <file>` restores the file, and you start the task over with a sharper prompt.

Because of option 3, make sure you commit before big agent sessions. A clean git state is your ultimate undo button.

## The golden rule of agent edits

Never let the agent edit code you do not understand at least roughly. You do not need to write every line yourself, but you need to be able to read the diff and judge it. If a diff is incomprehensible, ask Claude to explain it before approving:

```
Explain this diff to me line by line before I approve it.
```

This keeps you as the engineer in charge, with the agent as leverage, which is exactly the right relationship.

## Key takeaway

Files are the interface: Claude reads to understand, diffs to propose, and you review to approve. Be surgical in edit requests, scope explicitly, commit before big sessions, and never approve a diff you cannot roughly understand.

lessons.title: Permission Modes
lessons.bodyMd:
## Why permissions exist

Claude Code can read files, write files, delete files, and run shell commands. That is enormous power, and with it comes the obvious risk: an agent that misunderstands you could delete the wrong directory or push broken code. Permission modes are the dial that controls how much autonomy the agent gets. Learn them and you control the risk precisely.

## The four modes

### Ask before edits

Claude pauses and asks for approval before every file change. Nothing happens without your explicit yes. This is the default and the right choice when you are learning, working in an unfamiliar codebase, or touching anything high stakes like payment code or database migrations.

### Edit automatically

The agent applies edits to existing files on its own, but still asks before creating new files or running commands. This is the sweet spot for most day-to-day production work: the loop stays fast, and the remaining checkpoints catch the risky actions.

### Plan mode

Claude becomes read-only. It can explore your codebase, search the web, and think, but it cannot change a single file until you approve a written plan. This is the mode for complex builds and architecture decisions, and it gets its own deep-dive lesson next.

### Bypass permissions

Full autonomy. Claude can create, edit, delete, and run anything without asking. This is for advanced users doing rapid iteration or knowledge work where speed matters more than caution.

## Switching modes

You can change modes mid-session. In the terminal, press Shift+Tab to cycle through permission modes, or use the `/permissions` command to view and edit fine-grained tool permissions. In VS Code, the mode selector lives in the Claude panel.

A common rhythm looks like this: start a tricky task in Plan mode, approve the plan, switch to Edit automatically for the build, and drop to Bypass only for well-understood repetitive work.

## Enabling bypass safely

Bypass is powerful enough to deserve a deliberate opt-in. In VS Code, go to Extensions, find Claude Code, click the gear icon, open Settings, and enable the "dangerously skip permissions" option. The word "dangerously" is doing real work in that label.

The documented risk is blunt: with bypass on, a misunderstood instruction could theoretically delete your entire hard drive. This is rare, but it has happened to people. Rules for bypass:

- Only use it in folders you could afford to lose, or with clean git state and recent commits
- Never use it on your first session in a new codebase
- Keep backups of anything irreplaceable outside the working directory
- Turn it back off when the rapid iteration phase ends

## Recommended defaults by situation

| Situation | Recommended mode |
|---|---|
| Learning the tool | Ask before edits |
| Unfamiliar codebase | Ask before edits |
| Daily feature work | Edit automatically |
| Architecture or big refactor | Plan mode first |
| Repetitive, well-understood edits | Bypass (with git safety net) |
| Anything touching production data | Ask before edits, always |

## The permission mindset

Think of permission modes like the gears on a bike. Low gear (ask before edits) for steep, tricky terrain. High gear (bypass) for flat open road where you want speed. Nobody rides an entire route in one gear, and nobody should run every session in one mode. Shifting deliberately is the skill.

## Key takeaway

Four modes, one dial: ask, auto-edit, plan, bypass. Default to caution, shift up for speed when the terrain is safe, and treat bypass like a power tool with the safety off. Match the mode to the risk, not to your mood.

lessons.title: Plan Mode: The Most Important Mode
lessons.bodyMd:
## A minute of planning saves ten minutes of building

Here is the math that makes plan mode the highest-leverage habit in Claude Code. Without planning, a typical feature goes like this:

```
Build (15 min) -> Test (5 min) -> Fail -> Rebuild (15 min) -> Test (5 min) -> Fail...
```

Each cycle burns 35 minutes or more, and most of the rebuild time is rework that a five minute plan would have prevented. With plan mode:

```
Plan (5 min) -> Spot the flaw -> Replan (5 min) -> Build (15 min) -> Test (5 min) -> Done
```

One cycle, about 30 minutes, and the result is usually better because the design got a second pass before any code existed.

## What plan mode actually does

When you enter plan mode, Claude becomes read-only. It can:

- Read any file in your project
- Search the codebase and the web
- Run non-destructive commands (like listing directories)
- Think through approaches and tradeoffs

It cannot create, edit, or delete anything. When its research is done, it presents a plan document: the approach, the files it will touch, the order of operations, and the risks it sees. You review the plan, request changes, and only when you approve does it start building.

## When to reach for plan mode

Use plan mode whenever the task has any of these properties:

- **It touches more than three files.** Multi-file changes have interaction effects that deserve a design pass.
- **You are unsure of the approach.** If you cannot picture the solution, make the agent picture it first, cheaply.
- **It is a refactor.** Refactors look simple and hide dragons. A plan surfaces them.
- **Someone else will review the code.** A plan gives you a design artifact to discuss before the code exists.
- **The cost of being wrong is high.** Database migrations, auth changes, API contracts.

For a one-line typo fix, plan mode is overkill. For everything architecturally interesting, it is the default.

## How to run a great planning session

Enter plan mode, then prompt like this:

```
I need to add role-based access control to this app. Research how auth
currently works, then propose a plan: the data model changes, the
middleware approach, and which files you would touch, in order. Do not
write any code yet.
```

The "do not write any code yet" is redundant in plan mode (it cannot), but stating it keeps the agent's thinking focused on design rather than implementation details.

When the plan arrives, interrogate it:

- "What happens to existing users who have no role assigned?"
- "Why middleware instead of checking in each route handler?"
- "What is the rollback plan if the migration fails?"

This is the cheapest possible time to find flaws. A flaw found in the plan costs a sentence. The same flaw found after building costs an hour.

## The plan as documentation

Approved plans are useful beyond the build. Save the good ones. A plan document for a complex feature becomes onboarding material for the next developer, a reference when the feature needs changes six months later, and evidence of design thinking for code review. Some teams keep a `plans/` folder in the repo for exactly this.

## Exiting plan mode

Once you approve the plan, switch back to Edit automatically or Ask before edits and tell Claude to execute. Reference the plan explicitly:

```
Approved. Execute the plan, starting with the data model changes.
Run the test suite after each step.
```

The agent now builds with a clear roadmap instead of improvising. You will notice the difference immediately: fewer wrong turns, cleaner diffs, and a verification step that was designed in rather than bolted on.

## Key takeaway

Plan mode trades five minutes of thinking for hours of rework. Use it for anything multi-file, uncertain, or high stakes. Interrogate the plan hard, approve deliberately, then execute against it. This single habit will improve your output more than any other technique in this guide.

lessons.title: Choosing Your Model in Claude Code
lessons.bodyMd:
## Choosing Your Model in Claude Code

Claude Code ships with a smart default: Sonnet 5. Most of the time you should leave it there. But knowing when to switch up to Opus 4.8 or down to Haiku is one of the highest-leverage decisions in your workflow, because model choice drives both quality and cost. This lesson gives you the 2026 lineup and a simple decision rule.

## The 2026 lineup

**Sonnet 5** (June 2026) is the default model in Claude Code and on Anthropic's Free and Pro plans. Anthropic calls it the most agentic Sonnet yet: it makes plans, uses browsers and terminals, and runs autonomously at a level that required larger, more expensive models just months earlier. Its scores sit near Opus 4.8 (63.2% vs 69.2% on the agentic coding benchmark SWE-Bench Pro), a large jump over Sonnet 4.6's 58.1%. It checks its own output without being asked, refuses malicious requests more reliably, and shows lower hallucination and sycophancy than 4.6. Pricing is $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, and Anthropic has made that pricing permanent.

**Opus 4.8** (May 2026) is the top-tier model: the accuracy king for agentic coding and the hardest reasoning tasks. It leads the field at 69.2% on SWE-Bench Pro and 84% on OSWorld-Verified computer use, and it is about four times less likely than its predecessor to let flaws in its own code pass unremarked. When a task is long, ambiguous, and expensive to get wrong, Opus 4.8 is the model you want. It costs substantially more than Sonnet 5, so you spend it deliberately.

**Sonnet 4.6** (February 2026) is the previous generation, with a 1M token context window and solid coding and computer-use skills. If you spot it in older configs or examples, treat it as legacy: Sonnet 5 is a drop-in upgrade with meaningfully better agentic behavior.

**Haiku** is the fast, cheap tier: great for classification, extraction, mechanical checks, and anything high-volume where top reasoning is not needed.

## The default rule: do not switch

Here is the rule that covers 90% of sessions: stay on Sonnet 5. It was chosen as the default because it is the best value in the lineup: near-Opus agentic performance at a fraction of the price. If you are building features, fixing bugs, refactoring, or reviewing code, Sonnet 5 is the right model. Model switching is a power tool, not a daily habit.

## When to reach for Opus 4.8

Switch up when the problem is genuinely hard and the cost of being wrong is high:

- Architecture decisions with long-lived consequences
- Gnarly debugging where Sonnet 5 went in circles twice
- Planning a large migration or refactor in plan mode, then switching back to Sonnet 5 to execute the plan
- Tasks where maximum accuracy matters more than speed or cost

A common pattern: plan in Opus 4.8, build in Sonnet 5. You get the flagship's judgment on the design and the workhorse's economics on the execution.

## When Haiku is enough

Switch down for mechanical, high-volume work: lint-level reviews, bulk classification, simple extraction pipelines, routine CI checks. Prototype on Sonnet 5 and test whether Haiku handles the production workload; the cost difference at scale is enormous.

## How to switch mid-session

The `/model` command switches models without leaving your session:

```
/model
```

Pick from the list, or jump straight to the one you want. When the hard part is done, switch back. Most people spend the bulk of every session on Sonnet 5 and visit Opus 4.8 only for the hardest stretches.

## Two Sonnet 5 gotchas

First, Sonnet 5 runs adaptive thinking by default. You do not need to configure extended thinking, and if your scripts pass manual thinking settings or non-default sampling parameters (temperature, top_p, top_k), the API returns a 400 error instead of ignoring them. Strip those parameters when migrating older automation to Sonnet 5.

Second, pricing is simple but tokens add up in agentic sessions: long tool-use loops burn output tokens fast. Run `/cost` during a session to see where you stand, and remember that the cheapest model that does the job always wins.

## Key takeaway

Sonnet 5 is the default for a reason: it is the best value for daily work. Reach up to Opus 4.8 for the hardest reasoning, down to Haiku for mechanical volume, and check `/cost` when you are curious. Model choice is a dial, not a commitment.

lessons.title: CLAUDE.md: Your Project Brain
lessons.bodyMd:
## The file that steers every session

`CLAUDE.md` is a markdown file in your project root (or in `.claude/CLAUDE.md`) that gets injected at the very top of every conversation, before you even send your first message. It sets the trajectory for the entire session. Get it right and every session starts smart. Get it wrong and every session starts confused.

## The ship analogy

Think of your conversation as a ship leaving port. `CLAUDE.md` sets the initial heading. A one-degree error at departure is invisible at first, but by the destination you are 100 kilometers off target. Small imprecisions in this file compound across every message in the session. Precision here pays compound interest.

## Starting from zero: run /init

When you open Claude Code in a new folder, your first command should be:

```
/init
```

This scans the codebase and auto-generates a `CLAUDE.md` summarizing the project: what it does, how it is structured, how to build and test it. It is a solid first draft, not a finished product. Your job is to refine it.

## What a great CLAUDE.md contains

- **Project summary in three sentences.** What it is, who it is for, the tech stack.
- **Build and test commands.** `npm run dev`, `npm test`, whatever applies. This saves the agent from guessing.
- **Architecture notes.** "API routes live in src/api, shared logic in src/lib, never put business logic in components."
- **Guardrails.** "Never edit files in src/legacy. Always run tests before claiming done. Ask before adding dependencies."
- **Code style.** "TypeScript strict, no `any`, Tailwind for styling, functional components only."

Write it in bullet points with short headings. High information density beats elegant prose. The agent parses bullets better than paragraphs.

## The do's

- **Put the most important guardrails at the top.** Primacy bias is real: the model remembers the beginning of its context best. Your number one rule goes first.
- **Keep it 200 to 500 lines max.** Long enough to be useful, short enough to stay loaded cheaply in every session.
- **Treat it like living code.** Review it monthly. Delete rules that no longer apply. Add rules when the agent makes a repeated mistake.
- **Be specific.** "Run `npm test` after every change to src/api" beats "make sure things work."

## The don'ts

- **Do not dump entire style guides or API docs into it.** That is expensive (tokens in every session) and actually reduces quality by burying the important rules in noise.
- **Do not write vague rules.** "Be smart" and "make no mistakes" mean nothing. The agent cannot operationalize them.
- **Do not include files unnecessarily with @-mentions.** Every included file costs context in every session.
- **Do not let it bloat.** Agents love to append to CLAUDE.md. Prune it regularly or it becomes a 2,000-line junk drawer.

## The three layers

`CLAUDE.md` exists at three levels, and they stack:

1. **Global** (`~/CLAUDE.md` in your home folder): applies to every project. Put your universal preferences here: "I prefer TypeScript, I hate semicolons in prose, always explain before deleting."
2. **Project** (`.claude/CLAUDE.md` or `./CLAUDE.md`): specific to the current repo. Architecture, commands, guardrails.
3. **Enterprise** (managed at the system level): almost nobody uses this. Skip it unless your company mandates it.

Keep global truly global and project truly project-specific. When a rule only applies to one repo, it does not belong in your home folder.

## A starter template

```markdown
# Project: TaskFlow

TaskFlow is a task management app for small teams.
Stack: Next.js 14, TypeScript, Prisma, Postgres, Tailwind.

## Commands
- Dev: `npm run dev`
- Test: `npm test`
- Build: `npm run build`

## Architecture
- API routes in `src/app/api/`, business logic in `src/lib/`
- Never put database queries in React components
- All forms use React Hook Form + Zod validation

## Guardrails
- Never edit files in `src/legacy/`
- Always run tests after changing `src/lib/`
- Ask before adding a new npm dependency
```

Start from `/init` output, reshape it toward this, and iterate. After a week of real sessions you will know exactly which rules earn their place.

## Key takeaway

`CLAUDE.md` is the highest-leverage file in your workflow. Generate it with `/init`, keep it dense and specific, put guardrails first, cap it at 500 lines, and prune it like a garden. Every session you run pays rent on this file; make the rent worth it.

lessons.title: The .claude Directory
lessons.bodyMd:
## Beyond the single file

As projects grow, one `CLAUDE.md` starts to strain. The `.claude/` directory is the upgrade path: a structured home for project configuration, custom agents, skills, and rules. This lesson maps the whole directory so you know what lives where.

## The standard layout

```
.claude/
├── settings.json          # Team permissions, hooks
├── settings.local.json    # Your local overrides (gitignored)
├── CLAUDE.md              # The project brain
├── CLAUDE.local.md        # Your local additions (gitignored)
├── agents/                # Custom subagent definitions
├── skills/                # Reusable skill checklists
├── rules/                 # Component rules, split by topic
└── .mcp.json              # Model Context Protocol config
```

You do not need all of these on day one. Start with `CLAUDE.md` and `settings.local.json`, add the rest as needs arise.

## settings.json vs settings.local.json

`settings.json` is shared with your team through git. It holds project-wide configuration: default permission rules, hooks that run on certain events, and environment settings everyone should share.

`settings.local.json` is yours alone and gitignored. It holds your personal overrides: your preferred model, your permission tweaks, your local paths. When a teammate's config annoys you, override it here instead of arguing about the shared file.

A common pattern in `settings.json`:

```json
{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": ["Bash(npm test)", "Bash(npm run lint)"],
    "deny": ["Bash(rm -rf *)", "Read(.env)"]
  }
}
```

This pre-approves safe commands and hard-blocks dangerous ones for the whole team. The agent cannot talk its way around a deny rule, which is exactly the point.

## The rules folder: splitting the monolith

When `CLAUDE.md` creeps past 500 lines, split it. The `rules/` folder holds focused markdown files by topic:

- `rules/workflow.md`: how we build (branching, review process, deploy steps)
- `rules/technical-defaults.md`: code style, TypeScript config, testing expectations
- `rules/design-rules.md`: colors, spacing, component patterns

Each file stays short and focused. Benefits over one giant file:

- **Granular control.** Update the design rules without touching the workflow rules.
- **Easier collaboration.** Two people can edit different rule files without merge conflicts.
- **Better loading.** Related rules can be pulled in only when relevant, instead of one 10,000-word monster in every session.

## agents/ and skills/

The `agents/` folder holds custom subagent definitions: markdown files describing specialized agents your project uses repeatedly. The `skills/` folder holds reusable skill checklists. Both get full lessons later in this guide (subagents in this chapter, skills in Chapter 4). For now, just know where they live.

## .mcp.json: external integrations

This file configures Model Context Protocol servers: pre-built integrations that connect Claude to external tools like browsers, project trackers, and databases. MCP gets its own discussion in the context of skills in Chapter 4. The short version: MCP is great for quick prototyping, but for anything you use daily, convert it to a skill for 10 to 100 times better token efficiency.

## Hooks: automation on events

Hooks in `settings.json` run scripts when certain things happen: before a tool call, after a file edit, when a session starts. Practical uses:

- Auto-format code after every edit
- Run the linter after file writes and show Claude the errors immediately
- Log session activity for team visibility

Example hook that runs Prettier after edits:

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Write|Edit",
        "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "npx prettier --write $FILE" }]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

Hooks turn "remember to format" from a CLAUDE.md wish into an enforced behavior. Wishes get forgotten; hooks do not.

## Setting it up for a team

1. Commit `.claude/settings.json`, `.claude/CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/rules/`, and shared skills.
2. Gitignore `settings.local.json` and `CLAUDE.local.md` so personal tweaks never collide.
3. Document the setup in your README so new teammates get the full agent configuration on clone.

A new hire cloning the repo gets your entire AI workflow, not just the code. That is a genuine onboarding superpower.

## Key takeaway

`.claude/` is your project's agent operating system: shared settings, split rules, custom agents, skills, and hooks. Start small, split `CLAUDE.md` into `rules/` when it grows, gitignore the local files, and use hooks to enforce what matters.

lessons.title: Context Management
lessons.bodyMd:
## Context is your budget

Every Claude Code session runs inside a context window: a limited amount of text the model can consider at once. Think of it as a budget. Everything you and the agent do spends from it, and when it runs out, old information gets compressed or dropped. Managing this budget well is the difference between sharp sessions and confused ones.

## What eats your context

Run `/context` in any session to see a live breakdown. The typical overhead before you even send your first message is 35,000 to 45,000 tokens, roughly a quarter of the window. Here is where it goes:

1. **System prompt** (your CLAUDE.md plus rules): around 10,000 tokens
2. **System tools** (read, write, bash, web search definitions): around 17,000 tokens
3. **MCP tools**: variable, and bad ones can eat 20,000+ tokens alone
4. **Memory file**: Claude's persistent notes, usually tiny (under 100 tokens)
5. **Skills**: only front matter loads until invoked, about 60 tokens each
6. **Your messages**: the conversation itself, growing with every turn

The big lever is number 3. A single bloated MCP server can consume more context than your entire CLAUDE.md. This is why the guide keeps pushing skills over MCP: skills cost 60 tokens until used, MCP costs thousands upfront.

## Longer context is not better context

Newer models advertise enormous windows: 200,000 tokens, even millions. It is tempting to think more is always better. It is not. Research and practice both show that longer prompts reduce output quality. The model gets distracted, loses track of instructions buried in the middle, and produces vaguer work. A tight, focused 50,000-token context outperforms a sprawling 500,000-token one almost every time.

Your goal is not to fill the window. Your goal is to keep the relevant signal dense and the noise out.

## The essential commands

**`/compact`** compresses the conversation into a high-density summary, freeing context while preserving the important decisions and state. Use it when you feel the session getting sluggish or when `/context` shows usage above 70 percent. After compacting, restate your key constraints in one message to re-anchor the agent.

**`/clear`** wipes the conversation entirely and starts fresh. Use it when switching to an unrelated task. There is no benefit to keeping yesterday's authentication refactor in context while you work on today's landing page copy. Fresh is fast.

**`/cost`** shows your current token usage for the session. Check it when you are curious where the budget went, or when you suspect an MCP server is eating more than it should.

## High-ROI strategies

**Prefer skills over MCP.** Already covered, but it bears repeating: this single choice can save tens of thousands of tokens per session.

**Move instructions from CLAUDE.md into skills.** Anything the agent only needs sometimes (deployment steps, release checklists) belongs in a skill that loads on demand, not in the file that loads every session.

**Use cheaper models for subagents.** Subagents doing research or QA do not need the flagship model. Sonnet-class models are cheaper and have generous windows, perfect for parallel grunt work.

**Write specific prompts.** "Fix the null pointer in checkout.ts line 42" spends far less context on exploration than "improve the checkout flow." Specificity is a context-saving device.

**Front-load research with plan mode.** Get the exploration done in a read-only planning session, approve the design, then execute. Exploration during the build phase means expensive backtracking.

**Compress verbose input.** Got a 20-minute voice memo of ideas? Run it through a cheap model first for a tight summary, then bring the summary to your main session. Same ideas, a tenth of the tokens.

## Auto-compaction: the safety net

When you hit the buffer (usually around 33,000 tokens remaining), Claude automatically compresses older messages into denser summaries. This is a safety net, not a strategy. Auto-compaction keeps you moving, but it compresses blindly: it may keep trivia and drop the decision you actually needed. Manual `/compact` at a natural breakpoint, followed by your own two-sentence recap, beats the automatic version every time.

## The status line: your fuel gauge

In the terminal, run `/status` to configure a live status line showing your context percentage, current model, and git branch. It sits at the bottom of every session like a fuel gauge. Glance at it the way you glance at your phone battery: casually, often, and with a plan for what you will do when it runs low.

## Key takeaway

Context is a budget, not a warehouse. Watch it with `/context` and the status line, spend it with `/compact` and `/clear`, and keep it dense with skills, specific prompts, and plan-first research. Tight context means sharp output.

lessons.title: Subagents: Parallel Power
lessons.bodyMd:
## What subagents are

A subagent is a fresh Claude instance spawned from your session to handle one focused task. The critical detail: it starts with **zero context** from the parent. It does not know your conversation history, your CLAUDE.md debates, or what you tried an hour ago. It gets a task description, does the work in its own context window, and returns a summary to the parent.

That isolation is the whole point. It is also what makes subagents both powerful and tricky.

## The three most valuable subagents

**The Researcher.** Give it heavy research: web searches, documentation reading, data gathering across a codebase. Run it on a cheaper model (Sonnet 5) in parallel with your main work. Only a tight summary (around 2,000 tokens) returns to your expensive parent session. Users report roughly 50x cost savings versus doing deep research in the main thread.

**The Code Reviewer.** Ask it to review code the parent just wrote. Because it has zero context, it has zero bias. The parent agent carries 10,000+ tokens of "I wrote it this way because..." rationalization. The reviewer looks at the code cold and says "this is weird, why did you do it this way?" It catches issues the parent would never see in its own work.

**The QA Tester.** Have it generate and run tests against new code. Test execution stays out of the parent's context entirely; only pass/fail results and diffs come back. Your main session stays clean and focused on building.

## Parallelization math

Serial work adds up: three 1-minute tasks run one after another take 3 minutes. Three subagents running simultaneously take about 1 minute total. For independent tasks, parallel subagents are pure time savings.

But there is a catch, and it is mathematical. If each subagent succeeds 95 percent of the time:

- 3 subagents: about 86 percent chance all succeed
- 10 subagents: about 59 percent chance all succeed
- 50 subagents: about 7 percent chance all succeed

Every agent you add multiplies the failure probability. Keep subagent tasks simple and focused. A subagent asked to "research the auth library and summarize the API" will nail it. A subagent asked to "redesign the auth system, migrate the database, and update all call sites" will find creative new ways to fail.

## Spawning subagents well

The task description is everything, because it is the only context the subagent gets. Include:

- Exactly what to do, in concrete terms
- What a good result looks like
- What to return (a summary? a diff? a file?)
- Constraints ("read-only, do not modify files" for researchers)

Example of a good spawn:

```
Research how our project handles file uploads. Read src/upload/ and
related tests. Return: the upload flow in 5 bullet points, the
validation rules, and any security concerns you spot. Do not modify
any files.
```

Example of a bad spawn:

```
Look into uploads.
```

The bad one returns whatever the subagent found interesting, which may have nothing to do with what you needed.

## Agent teams: subagents on steroids

For work that needs discussion and debate rather than just parallel execution, there is a bigger pattern: agent teams. These are fully independent Claude Code instances that own their own context windows, can message each other directly (not just the parent), and self-coordinate through a shared task list.

Subagents report only to the parent. Agent teams collaborate with each other. That makes teams right for:

- **Design exploration:** three agents build three fundamentally different designs, then you pick a winner
- **Security auditing:** scanner agents sweep the codebase, debate agents argue findings, fixer agents patch
- **Product ideation:** proposal agents pitch features, critic agents argue pros and cons, consensus emerges

Enable them by adding to `settings.json`:

```json
{
  "env": {
    "CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS": "1"
  }
}
```

The cost warning is serious: agent teams consume roughly 7x the tokens of a standard session, and a 10-agent team in plan mode can burn through $80 in 15 minutes. Set spending limits. Use Sonnet 5 for teammates. Keep teams small. Reserve teams for problems where debate genuinely improves the answer.

## Git work trees: parallel without conflicts

When multiple agents need to touch the same repo, file conflicts get messy. Git work trees solve this: each agent gets its own folder and branch, works in isolation, and you merge the results at the end.

```
main -> hotfix branch (Agent 1: fix the bug)
     -> feature branch (Agent 2: build the feature)
     -> docs branch (Agent 3: write the docs)
     -> merge all back to main
```

Use work trees for parallel page development (about, contact, and pricing pages built simultaneously) or any multi-agent work where agents might otherwise edit the same files.

## Key takeaway

Subagents give you parallel execution with zero-context isolation: researchers save money, reviewers catch bias, QA keeps your main thread clean. Write tight task descriptions, keep tasks simple (failure multiplies), and reserve agent teams for work where debate beats parallelism. Watch the token bill.

lessons.title: The Golden Loop: Verify Everything
lessons.bodyMd:
## The loop most people skip

Here is the core building philosophy in one diagram:

```
TASK -> DO THE TASK -> VERIFY RESULTS -> REPEAT
```

Most people run a broken version:

```
TASK -> DO -> TASK -> DO (no verification)
```

They prompt, accept the output, prompt again. No checking. The code "looks right" so it must be right. Then production breaks at 2 AM and nobody knows which of the thirty unverified changes caused it.

The value of AI coding is not one-shot perfection. Humans are still better at getting it right the first time. The value is **speed of iteration**: going from 80 percent to 90 to 99 percent in minutes instead of hours. But iteration only works if each cycle includes verification. Otherwise you are iterating on illusions.

## What verification looks like

Verification means proving the change works, not feeling good about it. Pick the method that fits the task:

- **Automated tests.** The gold standard for logic. "Run the test suite" should be in nearly every build prompt.
- **Build checks.** Does it compile? Does TypeScript pass? Does the linter stay quiet?
- **Screenshot comparison.** For UI work: screenshot before, screenshot after, compare. Pixel-level truth.
- **Review subagent.** A fresh-eyes agent checking the parent's work (see the previous lesson).
- **Manual smoke test.** Actually click through the flow yourself for anything user-facing.

Tell the agent which verification you expect, every time:

```
Add a password strength meter to the signup form. When done, run the
component tests and take a screenshot of the form to confirm the
meter renders correctly.
```

## Three ways to build, ranked

**1. Reference design plus screenshot loop (best results).** Give Claude a screenshot or mockup plus the relevant styles. It builds a first version, screenshots its own output, compares against the reference, and iterates. This closed loop produces shockingly faithful reproductions because the agent can see its own mistakes.

**2. Voice transcript dump (fastest for ideas).** Talk through what you want at 200 words per minute into any transcription tool. Dump the transcript to Claude and let it extract the structure. Great for brainstorming and rough drafts; expect lower initial quality that you refine through the golden loop.

**3. Component libraries (fastest for standard UI).** Grab pre-built component prompts from libraries like 21st.dev, paste them in, assemble. Very fast for standard patterns (pricing tables, navbars, footers), but the result can feel generic and the pieces do not always cohere without iteration.

## Building verification into your defaults

Do not rely on remembering to ask. Make verification automatic:

- Put "always run tests after changing code" in your CLAUDE.md guardrails
- Add a post-edit hook that runs the linter automatically (Chapter 3, lesson 2)
- End complex prompts with an explicit verification instruction
- Use the QA subagent pattern for anything you cannot verify yourself

The goal is a workflow where unverified code feels wrong, like leaving the house without your keys. It should nag at you.

## The iteration mindset

Beginners treat each agent output as final and get frustrated when it is not perfect. Veterans treat each output as a draft and get excited about how fast the drafts improve. That mindset shift is everything.

A realistic session looks like this:

1. "Build the dashboard layout." (70 percent right)
2. "The sidebar is too wide and the cards need more padding." (85 percent)
3. "Match the card style to the reference screenshot." (95 percent)
4. "Run the tests, fix the two failures, screenshot the result." (done)

Four iterations, maybe ten minutes. A human would still be on step one. The agent's superpower is not quality per attempt; it is attempts per hour, with verification keeping each attempt honest.

## Key takeaway

Task, do, verify, repeat. Never skip verification: tests, builds, screenshots, or a reviewer. Pick your build method to fit the job, automate verification into your defaults, and think in drafts, not in final answers. Iteration speed is the whole game, and verification is what makes it safe.

lessons.title: Slash Commands You Will Use Daily
lessons.bodyMd:
## Your command palette

Slash commands are Claude Code's built-in shortcuts: quick actions you invoke with a forward slash instead of a full sentence. You have already met `/login` and `/init`. This lesson covers the full daily-driver set so the commands become reflexes.

## Session management

**`/init`** generates a `CLAUDE.md` from your current codebase. Run it once per new project, then refine the output by hand.

**`/clear`** wipes all conversation context and starts fresh. Use it when switching to an unrelated task. Old context is not wisdom; it is weight.

**`/compact`** compresses the conversation into a dense summary instead of wiping it. Use it mid-project when `/context` shows usage climbing past 70 percent. Follow it with a two-sentence recap of your key constraints.

**`/context`** shows the token breakdown: what is consuming your context window right now. Check it whenever a session feels sluggish or you suspect a tool is eating more than its share.

## Model and performance

**`/model`** switches between models mid-session: Opus 4.8 for the hardest reasoning, Sonnet 5 for the daily workhorse balance, Haiku for fast cheap tasks. A common pattern is planning in Opus 4.8, building in Sonnet 5. The Core Workflow chapter has a full lesson on choosing your model.

**`/cost`** shows token usage and estimated cost for the current session. No surprises on the bill.

**`/fast`** toggles fast mode: roughly 2.5x speed at roughly 3x cost. Useful when you are in a flow state and waiting feels expensive. Turn it off when the urgency passes.

## Permissions and account

**`/permissions`** opens the permission editor: view and change which tools the agent can use without asking. This is where you fine-tune the autonomy dial from Chapter 2.

**`/login`** and **`/logout`** manage authentication. **`/account`** shows your plan and usage status.

## Diagnostics

**`/status`** configures the terminal status line (context gauge, model, git branch). Set it up once and leave it on.

**`/debug`** enables debug output when something is behaving strangely. **`/insights`** shows analytics about your conversation patterns.

## The daily rhythm

A typical productive day touches maybe six of these:

```
Morning:  claude -c (resume) -> /context (check the budget)
Working:  /compact (when it gets heavy) -> /model (switch for hard parts)
Stuck:    /clear (fresh start on the new task)
Evening:  /cost (see what the day burned)
```

You do not need to memorize all of them today. Learn `/clear`, `/compact`, and `/context` first; they manage the resource everything else depends on. Add the rest as you feel the need.

## Commands vs skills vs MCP: the map

It helps to see how the three extension systems relate:

- **Slash commands** are built into Claude Code. They control the tool itself: sessions, models, permissions.
- **Skills** (next lesson) are your custom checklists for recurring work. They extend what the agent can do.
- **MCP** (covered in the skills lesson) connects pre-built third-party integrations. Fast to try, expensive to run daily.

Commands manage the session. Skills manage your workflows. MCP manages other people's tools. Each has its lane.

## Key takeaway

Slash commands are the control surface: `/clear`, `/compact`, and `/context` manage your session budget; `/model` and `/cost` manage power and spend; `/permissions` manages autonomy. Learn the session trio first and the rest will follow naturally.

lessons.title: What Skills Are (and Why They Beat MCP)
lessons.bodyMd:
## Reusable checklists for recurring work

A skill is a markdown file that teaches Claude Code how to do a specific recurring task, step by step. Think of it as a standard operating procedure (SOP) you write once, and the agent follows forever. Onboarding a new client, scraping and enriching leads, generating a weekly report: if you do it more than twice, it deserves a skill.

## The conductor and the musicians

A well-built skill has two parts, and the metaphor from the source material is worth keeping:

```
my-skill/
├── scripts/          # The musicians: Python/bash scripts that do the work
│   ├── scrape.py
│   └── enrich.py
└── skill.md          # The conductor: the checklist Claude follows
```

The scripts are dumb tools: they scrape a page, clean a CSV, call an API. The `skill.md` is the orchestrator: a step-by-step checklist telling Claude when to run which script, what to check, and what to do when something breaks. When a script fails, Claude uses its own intelligence to diagnose the problem, fix it, and update the skill so it works next time. Skills are self-healing in a way rigid automation never is.

## Why skills beat MCP

Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers are pre-built integrations other people made: connect Claude to your browser, your task tracker, your database with one line of JSON config. They are fantastic for quick experiments. But they have a structural cost problem.

An MCP server loads **all of its tool definitions** into your context window upfront, every session, whether you use them or not. A chatty MCP can eat 20,000 tokens before you type a word. A skill loads only its **front matter** (about 60 tokens) until you actually invoke it. The full checklist streams in on demand.

That makes skills 10 to 100 times more token-efficient than MCP for daily workflows. The practical pipeline the pros use:

1. **Install the MCP** to prototype fast (one line of JSON, immediate results)
2. **Test it**: can we do X, Y, Z reliably?
3. **Convert the working parts to a skill** using direct API calls instead of the bloated MCP server
4. **Delete the MCP config** and enjoy the reclaimed context

MCP is the sketchpad. Skills are the production line.

## What makes a skill economically valuable

The best skills automate work that is valuable, repetitive, and slightly messy: the kind of work where pure scripts break on edge cases but pure manual effort does not scale. Real examples:

- **Lead pipeline**: scrape prospects, verify contact info, enrich with firmographics, write to a spreadsheet
- **Literature research**: query PubMed with keywords, fetch abstracts, summarize findings by theme
- **Site generation**: take prospect data, generate a personalized one-page site in 30 seconds
- **Inbox triage**: label incoming mail, classify by urgency, draft replies for approval
- **Client onboarding**: send welcome emails, generate the kickoff doc, create the project folder structure

Notice the pattern: each one chains a few deterministic steps (scripts) with judgment calls (the agent). That combination is exactly where skills shine.

## The best MCP to know: Chrome DevTools

If you install one MCP, make it the Chrome DevTools integration. It gives Claude control of a live Chrome browser: navigate pages, click elements, take screenshots, extract text. It is roughly 100 times faster than older browser automation approaches, and it weaves beautifully into skill-based workflows (screenshot verification in the golden loop, for example). Prototype with it, then convert your stable flows to skills as described above.

## Where to find MCPs

Browse `mcp-servers.org` and `modelcontextprotocol.io/servers` for the official directory, plus various community marketplaces. Vet third-party servers carefully: an MCP runs code with your permissions, so a malicious or sloppy server is a genuine security risk. Prefer well-maintained servers with public source code and real user counts.

## Key takeaway

Skills are reusable SOP checklists: scripts do the deterministic work, `skill.md` conducts. They cost 60 tokens until invoked, versus thousands for MCP, so prototype with MCP and convert winners to skills. Target work that is valuable, repetitive, and slightly messy. That is where the return on investment lives.

lessons.title: Creating Your First Skill
lessons.bodyMd:
## From repeated chore to permanent asset

You have a task you do every week. Today you turn it into a skill. This lesson walks the full creation loop: draft, test cold, iterate to reliability.

## Step 1: Pick the right task

Good first skills are narrow and well-defined. "Generate my weekly status report from my git log and calendar" is a great first skill. "Handle all my project management" is not. You want something you can describe in five to ten bullet points, where each bullet is one concrete step.

Write the bullets yourself first. Example for a changelog skill:

- Read git log since the last tag
- Group commits by type: features, fixes, chores
- For each feature, write one plain-English sentence
- Format as markdown with sections
- Save to CHANGELOG.md under a new version heading
- Show me the draft before writing

If you cannot list the steps, you do not understand the task well enough to automate it yet. Do it manually once more, paying attention to your own process, then list the steps.

## Step 2: Let Claude draft the skill

Give Claude your bullet list and ask it to create the skill:

```
Create a skill called weekly-changelog in .claude/skills/weekly-changelog/.
It should do the following:
[paste your bullets]
Include a skill.md checklist and any scripts needed.
```

Claude will research the skill format if needed and produce the directory: `skill.md` with front matter (name, description, when to use it) plus the step-by-step checklist, and any helper scripts. Review the draft the way you would review code: is each step concrete? Are the edge cases handled? Is the "when to use this" description accurate? That description is what triggers the skill later, so make it precise.

## Step 3: The cold test

Here is the step most people skip, and it is the most important one. Take the finished skill to a **fresh Claude instance with zero context**: a new session, a different folder, no conversation history. Ask it to use the skill on a real example.

Why cold? Your main session is full of shared understanding that masks gaps in the skill. If the skill only works when you are there to fill in the blanks, it is not a skill yet, it is a reminder note. The cold test exposes every assumption you accidentally baked in.

## Step 4: Iterate to reliability

Expect the first cold test to land around 70 percent. That is normal. The iteration loop looks like this:

- **70 percent**: works with guidance, misses edge cases
- **80 percent**: handles the common cases solo
- **90 percent**: survives unusual inputs
- **98 percent**: trustworthy enough to run while you get coffee

Each round, take what broke, describe it to Claude, and have it update the skill. "It failed when there were no commits since the last tag; add a step that handles the empty case gracefully." The skill file is living documentation of everything the task taught you.

## Anatomy of a good skill.md

```markdown
---
name: weekly-changelog
description: Generates a CHANGELOG entry from git history since the last tag.
  Use when the user asks for a changelog, release notes, or "what changed".
---

# Weekly Changelog

## Steps
1. Run `git log $(git describe --tags --abbrev=0)..HEAD --oneline` to list commits.
2. If empty, report "no changes since last tag" and stop.
3. Group commits: features (feat:), fixes (fix:), chores (everything else).
4. Write one plain-English sentence per feature or fix.
5. Format as markdown under a new `## [Unreleased]` heading.
6. Show the draft to the user before writing to CHANGELOG.md.

## Edge cases
- No tags exist: use the full log, note it in the output.
- Merge commits: skip them, they add noise.
```

The front matter description is the trigger: when your request matches it, Claude loads the skill automatically. Make the description match how you would actually ask.

## Step 5: Share it

Skills live in `.claude/skills/`, which means they travel with the repo. Commit them. Your teammates get your automation on clone, and improvements anyone makes benefit everyone. A team skill library compounds like any good codebase.

## Key takeaway

List the steps, let Claude draft the skill, cold-test it in a fresh session, and iterate from 70 to 98 percent. The front matter description is the trigger, so write it like you talk. Commit skills to the repo; they are team assets, not personal shortcuts.

lessons.title: Custom Slash Commands for Your Workflow
lessons.bodyMd:
## Beyond the built-ins

Chapter 4 opened with Claude Code's built-in slash commands. But you can also create your own: custom commands that run your prompts, your skills, or your scripts with a single keystroke. If you type the same long prompt every day, it deserves to become a command.

## What custom commands are

A custom slash command is a markdown file in `.claude/commands/` (project-scoped) or your global Claude config (available everywhere). The filename becomes the command: `deploy-check.md` becomes `/deploy-check`. The file content is the prompt that runs when you invoke it.

A simple example, `.claude/commands/review.md`:

```markdown
Review the changes in the current git diff. For each change, check:
1. Does it match the project's code style in CLAUDE.md?
2. Are there any obvious bugs or edge cases?
3. Is anything over-engineered?

Report findings as a short list. Do not modify any files.
```

Now `/review` runs a consistent code review on demand, the same way every time, in every session.

## Commands that take arguments

Commands can accept arguments with a `$ARGUMENTS` placeholder. A flexible test command:

```markdown
Run the test suite for the module named $ARGUMENTS.
Report pass/fail per file, and show the first failure's full output.
Do not fix anything unless I ask.
```

Invoke it as `/test auth` and `$ARGUMENTS` becomes `auth`. One command, infinite targets. This pattern turns vague recurring requests into precise tools.

## Commands that chain skills

The real power move is a command that invokes a skill with your preferred options baked in. Suppose you built the changelog skill from the last lesson. A command can wrap it:

```markdown
Run the weekly-changelog skill. After generating the draft,
also suggest a version bump (patch, minor, or major) with reasoning.
```

Now `/ship-notes` is your entire release-notes workflow in eleven characters.

## Project commands vs global commands

- **Project** (`.claude/commands/`): committed to the repo, shared with the team. "How we do things here": `/deploy-check`, `/onboard`, `/release`.
- **Global** (your home config): personal productivity across all projects. "How I like to work": `/summarize`, `/explain-like-im-five`, `/triage`.

The same split as CLAUDE.md layers from Chapter 3. Project-specific in the repo, personal in your home folder, and never the twain shall confuse.

## Ideas worth stealing

Commands that earn their keep in real workflows:

- `/standup`: summarize yesterday's commits and today's plan from git log and open issues
- `/pr-desc`: generate a pull request description from the branch diff
- `/explain $ARGUMENTS`: explain a file or concept simply, no jargon
- `/deps`: check for outdated dependencies and summarize what changed upstream
- `/fresh-eyes`: run the reviewer subagent pattern on recent changes

Start with one. The moment you catch yourself typing the same paragraph-long prompt for the third time, stop and command-ify it. Future you will be grateful.

## Key takeaway

Custom slash commands turn repeated prompts into keystrokes: a markdown file whose name becomes the command. Use `$ARGUMENTS` for flexibility, chain skills for power, keep project commands in the repo and personal ones global. Command-ify any prompt you type three times.

lessons.title: Why Run Models Locally
lessons.bodyMd:
## The cloud is not the only option

Everything so far in this guide has used cloud models: your prompts travel to Anthropic's servers, the answer comes back. That is the right default for hard work. But there is a second option worth knowing: running open models on your own machine with Ollama. It is free, private, and surprisingly capable.

## What Ollama is

Ollama is a free, open-source tool that downloads and runs large language models locally on your computer. One command installs it, one command pulls a model, and you have a private AI running on your hardware with no account, no API key, and no per-token bill.

```bash
ollama run llama3.1
```

That is the whole getting-started story. The model downloads once, then runs offline forever.

## Why local matters: four reasons

**Privacy.** Your prompts never leave your machine. For proprietary code, unreleased products, client data, or anything under NDA, local models eliminate the "should I paste this into a cloud AI?" dilemma entirely.

**Cost.** Cloud models bill per token. Local models cost electricity. If you run thousands of small tasks a day (summarizing, classifying, drafting), the savings add up fast. Heavy reasoning still belongs in the cloud, but the long tail of small jobs is perfect for local.

**Offline.** Planes, remote cabins, flaky conference wifi. A local model works wherever your laptop works. Your AI setup stops depending on connectivity.

**Experimentation.** Want to try a weird prompt 200 times? Fine-tune on your own data? Test how a different model handles your task? Local models make experimentation free and instant, no budget meetings required.

## The honest tradeoffs

Local models are not a replacement for Claude. Be clear-eyed about the gap:

- **Capability.** The best open models are excellent at focused tasks but still trail frontier cloud models on complex reasoning, long-context work, and nuanced code generation.
- **Hardware.** Bigger models need more RAM. A 7-8 billion parameter model runs fine on 16GB; the 70B monsters want 64GB or more. Apple Silicon Macs punch above their weight here (next lesson).
- **Speed.** Tokens per second depend on your chip. Modern machines are fast enough for interactive use with mid-size models; huge models can feel sluggish.

The winning pattern is not local *or* cloud. It is local *and* cloud: frontier models for the hard stuff, local models for the high-volume small stuff.

## Where local models fit in your workflow

- **Drafting.** Let a local model write the first draft of docs, emails, or boilerplate; refine in Claude Code.
- **Classification and triage.** Sort tickets, label emails, tag content: high volume, low reasoning.
- **Summarization.** Compress long transcripts, logs, or articles before bringing the summary to your main session (a context-saving trick from Chapter 3).
- **Privacy-sensitive work.** Anything you would hesitate to paste into a cloud prompt.
- **Learning.** Experiment freely with prompting techniques at zero marginal cost.

## The mental model

Think of cloud models as hiring a brilliant consultant: expensive per hour, worth it for the hard problems. Local models are the capable assistant who sits at the next desk: always available, free to bother, perfect for the steady stream of smaller jobs. You want both on your team.

## Key takeaway

Ollama puts capable AI on your own hardware: private, free, offline. It does not replace Claude Code's cloud models; it complements them. Use local for high-volume small tasks and anything sensitive; use cloud for hard reasoning. The hybrid setup is the professional setup.

lessons.title: Installing Ollama and Your First Model
lessons.bodyMd:
## Five minutes to a private AI

This lesson gets Ollama running on your machine and puts your first model to work. The whole process takes about five minutes plus download time.

## Step 1: Install Ollama

**Mac and Windows:** download the installer from ollama.com and run it. It sets everything up, including a menu bar icon.

**Linux:** one command in the terminal:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh
```

Verify the install:

```bash
ollama --version
```

You should see a version number. If the command is not found, restart your terminal so the new path loads.

## Step 2: Pull your first model

Models are downloaded with `ollama pull`, but you rarely need that command directly: `ollama run` downloads the model automatically on first use. Start with a solid general-purpose model:

```bash
ollama run llama3.1
```

The first run downloads several gigabytes, so grab a coffee. Every run after that starts in seconds. You are now chatting with an AI running entirely on your hardware. Try it:

```
>>> Explain what a REST API is in two sentences.
```

No account, no API key, no network calls. That prompt never left your machine.

## Step 3: Pick the right model size

Ollama hosts dozens of models, and size matters. The pattern is simple: bigger models are smarter but need more RAM and run slower.

| Your RAM | Comfortable model size | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| 8 GB | 3-4B parameters | llama3.2:3b, phi3 |
| 16 GB | 7-8B parameters | llama3.1:8b, mistral:7b |
| 32 GB | 13-34B parameters | llama3.1, codestral |
| 64 GB+ | 70B parameters | llama3.1:70b |

Start one tier below what your machine can handle; a fast 8B model you actually use beats a slow 70B model you avoid. For coding specifically, code-specialized models like `codestral` or `deepseek-coder` punch above their size.

Browse the full library at ollama.com/library. Each model page shows sizes, specialties, and the exact `ollama run` command.

## Step 4: The essential commands

```bash
ollama run llama3.1        # chat with a model (downloads if needed)
ollama list                # show downloaded models
ollama pull mistral        # download without running
ollama rm old-model        # delete a model to free disk space
ollama ps                  # show currently running models
```

Models stay loaded in memory after use for fast follow-up prompts. `ollama ps` shows what is resident; Ollama unloads idle models automatically when memory gets tight.

## Using Ollama from scripts

The real power for builders is the API. Ollama serves a local HTTP endpoint compatible with the OpenAI chat format:

```bash
curl http://localhost:11434/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "llama3.1",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize this: ..."}]
  }'
```

Any tool that speaks the OpenAI API format can point at `localhost:11434` instead. That includes custom scripts, editor plugins, and automation pipelines. Chapter 6 builds on this for scripting.

## Keeping models fresh

Open models improve constantly. Update a model with:

```bash
ollama pull llama3.1
```
